entries.meaning: Will and protection
entries.note: Its two roots refer to will and a protective helmet.

entries.meaning: The willow tree
A small songbird
From Old English wæd (“a ford”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From the Old English personal name Wæddi + -s- + worþ (“enclosure”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic وَحِيد (waḥīd).
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Waldemar in the 19th century. Compare Vladimir, from Slavic, and the Scandinavian name Valdemar.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From Old English walh (“Welshman”), genitive plural wala + denu (“valley”).
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: English surname, from the obsolete English given name Waltheof, from Old English weald (“power”) + þēof (“thief”), as in "one who snatched victory from battle." Comparable to, or ultimately Anglicized from, the Old Norse equivalent Valthiófr, from vald + *ᚦᛖᚢᛒᚨᛉ (*þeubaʀ). Compare Walthall, Waldie.
entries.note: A male given name from Old English, in modern American use transferred back from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Arabic وَلِيد (walīd).
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic, variant of Walid.

entries.meaning: From Arabic وَلِيد (walīd).
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic, variant of Walid.

entries.meaning: From Arabic وَلِيد (walīd).
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: An Old English byname for a Welshman or Breton, from Anglo-Norman waleis (“foreign”); see wǣlisċ.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, of 19th century and later usage.

entries.meaning: * (surname): The surname is an Old English byname for a Welshman or Breton, from Old French waleis (“foreign”). The Welsh hamlet may be derived from this.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Variant of Wayland or Waylon.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Walter. The derogatory British sense is a reference to the fictional character Walter Mitty from The Secret Life of Walter Mitty, a mild-mannered pushover who has wild fantasies about his life in various daring roles.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Walter.

entries.meaning: A Germanic name, from Middle English Walter, from Old Northern French Waltier, from Frankish *Waltheri (compare Old High German Waltheri, which see for more details), from Proto-West Germanic *Waldahari, from Proto-Germanic *Waldaharjaz, from *waldą (“ruler”) + *harjaz (“army, host”). Related to Old English Waldhere. Compare herald and Harold, in which these elements are reversed.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From Walter + -s.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Polish Wanda, possibly derived from an ethnic term for “a Wend”.
entries.note: A female given name from Polish.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Manipuri ꯋꯥꯡꯄꯨꯂꯦꯟ (wāngpulen).
entries.note: A male given name from Manipuri.

entries.meaning: * As an English surname, from the noun ward and related cognates such as warden, guard etc. * As an Irish surname, reduced from McWard, from mac an bard (“son of the poet”). * As a Jewish surname, adapted from Warshawski, named after Warsaw. Comparable to Warszawski. * As a French surname, Americanized from Guerin.
entries.note: An English male given name.

entries.meaning: * English, Norman, and German surname, all corresponding to German Werner. Also see Warrener. * As an Irish surname, Anglicized from Ó Murnáin (“descendant of Murnán”); see Murnane.
entries.note: A surname. A surname originating as a patronymic derived from a medieval given name, from Germanic war, warin "cautious; heedful; wary; watchful" + her, heri "army", modern German Werner.

entries.meaning: From the Anglo-Norman surname (de) Warenne, a reference to a place called Varenne, a hamlet near Arques-la-Bataille, along the river Varenne in Normandy, from Medieval Latin Warinna, a hydronym of Celtic/Gaulish origin, from *var-, *ver- (“river, water”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer- (“water, rain, flow”); see also the Latin river Avara. Phonetic Germanic influence is shown by the [v] > [w].
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Washington.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Washington.

entries.meaning: Washington (the town in Tyne and Wear, northeast England): probably from the Old English place name Hwæssingatūn (literally “a settlement of the household of *Hwæssa”), from *Hwæssa (a Saxon chieftain's name) + -ing (“belonging to”) + tūn (“homestead, settlement”). It was attested in 1096 as Wasindone.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, popular during the first century of American independence, given in honor of George Washington.

entries.meaning: Ultimately from Arabic وَسِيم (wasīm, literally “handsome, graceful”).
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: From a medieval diminutive of the given name Walter + the patronymic suffix -s.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Thai.
entries.note: A transliteration of a Thai female given name

entries.meaning: Patronymic surname from the Middle English given name Wat, derived from Walter, equivalent to Watt + -s.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Variant of Wayland popularized by the American singer Waylon Jennings who was originally named Wayland.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: An occupational surname for a cartwright, Old English wægen (“wagon”). Cf. wain.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Warren + -zza.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Warren.

entries.meaning: Using the suffix -y.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Webster.

entries.meaning: From Old English wella, genitive plural of well (“spring”), in reference to a residence near a group of springs. The original use of the genitive case here would've indicated origin. The -s ending of the modern form would be added later on upon reanalysis after the breakdown of the case system (outside of pronouns) that occurred in the development of English.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From French Wenceslas (variant of Venceslas), from Medieval Latin Wenceslaus.
entries.note: A male given name from the Slavic languages.

entries.meaning: From Latin Wenceslaus, a Latinization of Old Czech Vácslav, from Proto-Slavic *Vęťeslavъ (from *vęťьjь (“greater, more”) + *slava (“fame, glory”)). Doublet of Vyacheslav.
entries.note: A male given name from the Slavic languages.

entries.meaning: Short form of Germanic compound names beginning with the tribal name Wendel-, "a Wend".
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages transferred back from the surname.
entries.origin: the Germanic languages transferred back from the surname

entries.meaning: A spelling variant of Wendy.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: Popularized by the character in J. M. Barrie's play, Peter Pan (1904), though occasionally found earlier; the author explained that he got it from Fwendy-Wendy ("friend"), a nickname given to him by a child. Alternatively, from a diminutive of the Welsh Gwendolen; or from Wendelin, a diminutive of Wendel; therefore a doublet of Gwen.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Several places in England, from Old English west (“west”) + lēah (“wood, clearing”). Equivalent to west + -ley (“lea”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, of 18th century and later usage, today often without any religious connotations.

entries.meaning: A patronymic surname from Wes + -son, literally son of Wes, the latter a diminutive of the male given name Wesley.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From Old English hwītan, dative of hwīt (“white”) + īeġ (“island”), "white island".
entries.note: A female given name transferred from the surname, popular in the 1980s and 1990s due to the fame of Whitney Houston.

entries.meaning: From Old English Wīdsīþ.
entries.note: A given name.

entries.meaning: From an Old English female given name Wilburg, from wil (“will”) + burh (“fortress”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Will + -cock (“a medieval diminutive suffix”)
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name William.

entries.meaning: From Middle English wile, an occupational surname for a trapper or a nickname for a wily person.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Shortening.
entries.note: A male given name, diminutive of Wilfred.

entries.meaning: The name of two early Anglo-Saxon saints Wilfriþ, from Old English wil (“will”) + friþ (“peace”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old English, popular in the U.K. in the early twentieth century.

entries.meaning: Inherited from Old English Wilfriþ, from wil (“will”) + friþ (“peace”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old English, a less common form of Wilfred.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Wilhelm. Doublet of William.
entries.note: A male given name from German, equivalent to English William.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Wilhelmina, equivalent to Wilhelm + -ina.
entries.note: A female given name from German, masculine equivalent Wilhelm.

entries.meaning: From a Scottish diminutive of Wilk, a back-formation from Wilkin.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, in modern use often transferred back from the surname.

entries.meaning: Clipping of William or Willow, less often, other given names beginning with Wil-, such as Wilfred or Willard.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name William or, less often, other given names beginning with Wil-, such as Wilfred or Willard, from the Germanic languages; also used as a formal given name.

entries.meaning: Derived from Wilhelmina and recoined in the 19th century in America based on the male given names Will and William.
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From Old English wil (“will”) + heard (“brave, strong”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old English of mostly American usage. Partly transferred back from the surname.
entries.origin: Old English of mostly American usage

entries.meaning: From William + -ina.
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages, a rare feminine form of William, best known in Scotland.

entries.meaning: From a diminutive form of the personal name William.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: A pet form of the personal name William.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From Old English weliġ (“willow”) and Old Norse byr (“settlement”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From the clipping of William + -s (hypocoristic suffix).
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name William.

entries.meaning: From Old English willa (“mind, will, determination, purpose, desire, wish”) + mǣre (“famous”), from Proto-Germanic *Wiljamērijaz, from *wiljô + *mērijaz.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From Will (short form of William) + -son.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Winston.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Winston.

entries.meaning: Inherited from Middle English Wyndelsore, from Old English Windlesōra (“Windsor”, literally “bank with a windlass, winch by the riverside”), from *windel ("reel, winch"; > Middle English windel (“reel, spool”)) + ōra (“bank, shore”). See windlass.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Often a diminutive of names starting with Wi-, such as Wilhelmina and Winifred, with -y. Influenced by windy.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Old English Wynnfriþ, from wynn (“joy”) + friþ (“peace”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old English.

entries.meaning: From a medieval variant of Winfred.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From Old English Winfriþ, from Welsh Gwenfrewi.
entries.note: A female given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: Diminutive of Winifred used in 18th- and 19th-century America.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Diminutives + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Winifred or, less often, of Winona.

entries.meaning: From Dakota winúŋna (“firstborn daughter”). While not originally used as a personal name by the Dakota, it has been adopted as such by English speakers. John Koontz suggested that the name was a compound of wi- (“female”) + no (“first”) + -na (a diminutive suffix) and thus a reflex of Proto-Siouan *rǫ/*nǫ (“one”).
entries.note: A female given name from Dakota, used mainly in the United States.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Wynselowe, from Old English Wineshlǣw, from Wines (“Wine's”, personal name) + hlāw (“mound”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Old English personal name Wine, in the genitive singular case Wines + tūn (“farm, village”).
entries.note: A male given name derived from the place name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Wladimir.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From Middle English and German short forms of given names containing the Germanic element "wolf".
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Wolfgang (reinforced by Medieval Latin Wolfgangus), from Middle High German Wolfgang, from Old High German Wolfgang, from wolf (“wolf”) + gang (“path, course”).
entries.note: A male given name from German.

entries.meaning: From wood + row.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, given in the 1910s in honor of President Woodrow Wilson.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Woodrow + -y.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Woodrow.

entries.meaning: Ultimately from the Old English personal name Wigheard, from wīg (“war”) + heard (“hard, brave”), later also used as a Middle English diminutive of the names Guy and William.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, modern transferred use of the surname.

entries.meaning: From Welsh gwyn.
entries.note: A male given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: From the Welsh surname, from the name Gwyn. Also spelled as Wynne. Doublet of Gwynne.
entries.note: A unisex given name.

entries.meaning: Spelling variant of Wynn
entries.note: A male given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: Rare spelling variant of Winter.
entries.note: A female given name from English of modern usage.
